body: claimed: mkinney (Claude agent, M3) · 2026-11-09T02:37Z · plan: research first (no branch yet) - how controllers do chip-breaking on threads (multi-pass infeed, spring passes, interrupted passes and re-sync), what is safe to post, and a proposed split; posted here for the owner before any code

## Research: peck (chip-breaking) threading - what exists, what is safe to post, proposed split

Research only (no branch, no code). Sources are public vendor programming references, tooling-maker knowledge pages and the LinuxCNC reference, used for behaviour only, per the Clean-Room Protocol. No CAM post or CAM output was consulted.

### 1. What CamCraft does today

- **Kernel** `crates/motion/src/turning/thread.rs`: single-point, full-form V insert, external, straight thread only. The passes come from `blade::rungs(root, crest, infeed, 0)`, an **equal radial depth per pass** (`infeed`) from just under the crest down to the root, with **straight radial infeed** (each pass plunges square to the axis at the same lattice station). Each pass is one synchronized helix, written in CL as XY half-turn arcs about the axis (half a pitch each), with a rapid out to clearance at the end of the pass. It has no finish allowance, no spring pass, no flank or alternating infeed and no chip-break motion.
- **Op params** (`OpParams::Threading`): pitch, depth, infeed, feed, plunge feed, heights and tolerance. The insert width and included angle come from the tool.
- **Cycle record** `crates/cl/src/cl/thread.rs` (`ThreadCycle`, #34): already has fields for `first_depth`, `min_depth`, `finish_allowance`, `infeed_angle`, `spring_passes` and `pull_out`, but the kernel always fills them with radial / 0 / 0 / 0 (`attach_cycle`).
- **Post** `assets/posts/fanuc-lathe.cps` (our only lathe post; Tormach, Haas, Mazak, Sinumerik and Heidenhain are all mill posts) has two outputs, set by the `ThreadingOutput` post option:
  - `G32Passes` (the default) posts each half-turn as a **chained** `G32 Z.. F<lead>` block, so we already rely on consecutive G32 blocks keeping sync.
  - `G76Cycle` writes the two-block `G76 P(m)(r)(a) Q(dmin) R(d)` / `G76 X Z P(k) Q(Δd) F`, with m = 1 + spring passes, r = pull-out, a = 0/29/30/55/60/80 and the passes skipped. It refuses a record it cannot express.
- **A gap found on the way:** the G76 output and the verified passes do not describe the same pass schedule. The control's G76 sets each pass's depth from the first-pass depth Δd and the pass number n (Δd·√n, constant chip area), clamped at Δdmin. We post `Q = infeed` as the first depth, so the control cuts a **decreasing** ladder, while the simulator and verdict judged our **equal-depth** ladder. The final form and root are the same, so this is not a gouge. But the passes are documented as "the truth for verification", and with G76 chosen they are not what the machine does. This is filed below as sub-issue (b).
- **Milling** `crates/motion/src/machining2d/thread_mill.rs` (helical thread milling) is an interrupted cut by nature: each flute leaves a short chip. "Peck threading" does not apply to it. The nearest milling knob is the existing radial `infeed` per turn. Out of scope here.
- **Turning chip-break for comparison:** the groove kernels (`blade::plunge`) already retract fully to clearance after every rung (a full-retract peck). We do not post G74/G75 peck cycles.

### 2. How chip control on single-point threading is normally done

1. **Infeed method.** Radial infeed gives a stiff V-shaped chip that is "difficult to form and control". Modified flank (a compound angle a little under half the included angle, e.g. 29-29.5° for a 60° thread) is "the first choice method, giving the longest tool life and best chip control", because the chip forms on one side only. Alternating flank spreads wear across both edges but is harder to program. Sources: [Sandvik - choosing infeed method](https://www.sandvik.coromant.com/en-gb/knowledge/threading/thread-turning/how-to-choose-infeed-method-in-thread-turning-operations), [Sandvik - application tips](https://www.sandvik.coromant.com/en-gb/knowledge/threading/thread-turning/thread-turning-application-tips), [ISCAR threading handbook p.116-117](https://iscar.com/Catalogs/flipview/reference-user-guides/Threading_Handbook/files/basic-html/page117.html), [MMS - Threading on a lathe](https://mmsonline.com/articles/threading-on-a-lathe).
2. **Depth per pass.** Decreasing depth (constant chip area) is the default: "keep the first pass the deepest and the last pass around 0.07 mm", and avoid infeed under 0.05 mm. Constant depth "can give better chip control" but should not be used above about 1.5 mm pitch (Sandvik, same page). CamCraft today offers **only** constant depth.
3. **Spring passes.** These are extra passes at full depth. Sandvik "strongly recommend[s] against" them by default, for thread quality and insert life. Controls still offer them: LinuxCNC `H`, Fanuc-style G76 `m`. So they should be an option that defaults to 0.
4. **What the canned cycles already offer.**
   - **Fanuc-style two-block G76:** `P(m)(r)(a)` = finishing passes, pull-out chamfer in 0.1-lead steps, tool angle (00/29/30/55/60/80). `Q` = Δdmin, the minimum depth per pass. `R` = d, the finish allowance. Second block: `X Z R(i taper) P(k thread height) Q(Δd first depth) F(lead)`, with depth per pass by Δd·√n. Sources: [GSK988TA manual, G76 (Fanuc-compatible)](https://manualslib.com/manual/1767425/Gsk-Gsk988ta.html?page=124), [CTE - single-point thread programming](https://ctemag.com/node/23470). This is what our post's header already specs.
   - **Haas G76** (one block): `D` first-pass depth then D·√N, `K` height, `A` tool angle, and `P1-P4` = single-edge or double-edge (alternating) × constant amount or constant depth. Source: [Haas G76 reference](https://www.haascnc.com/service/codes-settings.type=gcode.machine=lathe.value=G76.html).
   - **LinuxCNC G76:** `J` first depth, `K` full depth, `R` depth degression (1.0 constant depth, 2.0 constant area), `Q` compound angle, `H` spring passes, `E`/`L` taper ends. Source: [LinuxCNC G-code reference, G76](https://linuxcnc.org/docs/html/gcode/g-code.html).
   - **What no cycle offers:** none of these cycles has an in-pass chip break or a per-depth repeat pass. Both have to be explicit synchronized blocks.

### 3. Can the tool pull out mid-pass and re-engage safely?

The thread exists only while axial feed stays locked to spindle angle. Three ways to do it:

- **Restarting a new threading move part-way along the thread: NOT safe, refused.** Every synchronized start waits for the index pulse, so the start phase is right ("waits for the spindle index ... so multiple passes line up", LinuxCNC). But the axis then accelerates from rest. LinuxCNC says it corrects so that Z "will reach the correct position just as it finishes accelerating", which means **the lead is wrong during the acceleration distance**. At the normal start that distance is in air, which is why threads need an approach length. Mid-thread it would run inside the groove already cut, putting the flank in the wrong place: a gouge. Haas G32 `Q` (start angle, 0.001°) and multi-start Z-shifts select a *phase*. They do not remove the ramp-up, so they do not make a mid-thread restart safe either. Sources: [LinuxCNC G33/G76](https://linuxcnc.org/docs/html/gcode/g-code.html), [Haas G32 reference](https://www.haascnc.com/service/codes-settings.type=gcode.machine=lathe.value=G32.html).
- **Control-side interrupt features are not chip breakers.** Siemens `LFON`/`LFOF`/`DILF` enable a "fast retraction for thread cutting (G33)" with a set lift distance. The manual describes it as an interrupt lift and documents no re-entry ([840D sl manual p.1323](https://manualslib.com/manual/1636342/Siemens-Sinumerik-840d-Sl.html?page=1323)). Feed hold during threading is not a usable mechanism either. Neither is something a CAM may post as a chip-break.
- **A dip inside one continuous synchronized chain: possible, but needs a confirmed citation before code.** Haas documents that sync is taken at the first G32 line and "stays in effect for each subsequent G32 line". Fanuc controls call this continuous thread cutting (consecutive G32 blocks with no deceleration). A G32 block may move X and Z together (a taper thread segment). So a chain like `G32 Z(a) F` → `G32 X(out by Δ) Z(a+s)` → `G32 X(back) Z(a+2s)` → `G32 Z(end)` keeps the phase the whole way, with no new index wait.
  - **Why it does not gouge:**
    - The pull-out is outward along the infeed vector by at most the current depth of cut, so the flanks lift onto the previous pass's surface.
    - Re-entry returns to the same commanded depth.
    - X servo lag can only make the dip shallower or later. It can never move the tool deeper than the pass depth, or move the helix.
    - Re-entry leaves a ramp-shaped wedge uncut, which is exactly the "high spots" the request wants a spring pass at that depth to clean.
  - **Evidence that this is done in industry:** Sandvik's CoroPlus OptiThreading puts an in/out oscillation into ordinary NC code on "existing and older CNC turning machines from a range of brands", with "interrupted cuts on all passes except the last one" ([Production Machining](https://www.productionmachining.com/articles/software-controls-chip-breaking-in-thread-turning-operations)). The article does not document *how* sync is kept, so we must not infer its method. Our basis has to be the controls' own documented continuous-threading rule.
  - **Caveats:**
    - Continuous-threading behaviour is documented above from Haas. For Fanuc it is so far only a secondary source ([continuous thread cutting, 18i](https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/g32-threading-servo-lag-continuous-thread-cutting-solution-for-fanuc-18i)). The primary Fanuc operator-manual section has to be cited before any post emits dips.
    - For LinuxCNC, whether consecutive G33 blocks wait for index again is not stated on the reference page. That is unconfirmed, so a LinuxCNC post must refuse dips until it is confirmed.
    - **G76 cannot express a dip**, so with `G76Cycle` chosen the post must refuse the option by name.

**Conclusion:**
- Mid-pass chip breaking is safe to post **only** as radial-out/radial-in segments inside one unbroken synchronized G32 chain, on a post that declares continuous threading, and verified like any other motion.
- Splitting the thread length into separately started threading moves is **never** posted.
- Neither is anything that relies on feed hold or a control's fast-lift.

### 4. Recommendation

The biggest gain for stainless and HRSA chip control is the standard toolkit, and it is cheap and documented: modified-flank or alternating infeed, a decreasing (constant-area) schedule with a minimum depth, a finish allowance and optional spring passes. Ship that first, for both G32 passes and G76 output, so the record's existing fields stop being hard-wired to 0. Add the per-depth repeat pass the request asks for as a G32-only option. Do the in-pass dip last, behind a post capability flag, once the Fanuc continuous-threading citation is in hand. The dip needs a new CL shape: today an XY arc must be a constant-radius half-turn, so the dip needs a variable-radius synchronized segment, plus simulator and verdict support. That makes it the expensive piece.

### 5. Proposed sub-issues (each `enhancement`, `area:turning` + `area:post` where relevant, `source:agent`, "Part of #363")

**(a) Threading: infeed method and decreasing-depth pass schedule** - P1
Add op params:
- infeed method: radial, modified flank with an angle, or alternating flank
- first-pass depth
- schedule: constant depth, or constant area by √n
- minimum depth per pass
- finish allowance
- spring passes at full depth (default 0)

The kernel lays the passes from these. Flank infeed shifts each pass's station by depth·tan(angle) on the helix lattice, and the verdict reads the shifted V. `attach_cycle` fills the `ThreadCycle` fields from them.
*Done means:* G32-pass output and the CL verdict follow each method and schedule. Pinning tests show the pass depths (√n with the Δdmin clamp), the flank station shift, and the spring-pass count for radial, flank and alternating infeed. The verdict stays clean on the modeled-thread fixture. A flank angle that does not fit the insert's included angle is refused at command creation. Changelog line.

**(b) G76 output describes the passes that were verified** - P1 (correctness of the verification claim; not a gouge)
With `G76Cycle`, the explicit passes have to match the control's own schedule: Δd·√n clamped at Δdmin, finish allowance d, m-1 spring passes, tool angle a as modified flank. The record maps 1:1 to `P(m)(r)(a) Q R` / `P(k) Q(Δd)`. Anything the cycle cannot express is refused by name: alternating infeed, per-depth repeats, dips, angles outside 0/29/30/55/60/80.
*Done means:* a golden G76 test where the simulated pass depths equal the control's √n sequence for the same words, plus a refusal test per unexpressible option. Depends on (a).

**(c) Per-depth repeat ("spring at each depth")** - P2
Optional: cut each roughing depth twice (same station, same depth) before stepping to the next depth, as the request describes. Defaults off, with a note that the tooling makers recommend against routine spring passes. G32 passes only, and G76 refuses it.
*Done means:* a pass-count and depth pinning test, plus a G76 refusal test.

**(d) In-pass chip-break dips inside a continuous synchronized chain** - P2
Params: dip interval (axial, at least N leads), dip height (at most the current pass's depth of cut, along the infeed vector), and dip length.
- Never on the first approach lead or the last lead; never on the finish or spring passes.
- New CL segment: a synchronized move with a radius change, plus simulator and verdict support.
- Posts declare `continuousThreading`. fanuc-lathe G32 emits the dip as `G32 X Z F` segments. G76 and posts without the flag refuse by name.

*Done means:*
- The primary-source citation for Fanuc continuous thread cutting is recorded in the post header before the code lands.
- Pinning tests: the dip never goes deeper than the pass depth; the phase (station mod lead) is unchanged across the chain; a dip within the approach or exit length, or on the finish pass, is refused; G76 refuses.
- Golden G32 output.

**Explicitly out of scope and refused, not filed:** restarting a threading move part-way along the thread (index re-sync with an acceleration ramp inside the groove = wrong lead = gouge); chip-breaking through feed hold or a control's fast-lift (LFON-type) features; oscillation methods whose sync rule is not publicly documented.

Filed the split from the research above: #416 (a, infeed method and decreasing-depth schedule, P1), #417 (b, G76 output matches the verified passes, P1, depends on #416), #418 (c, repeat pass at each depth, P2), #419 (d, in-pass dips in a continuous G32 chain, P2; needs the primary Fanuc citation first). Restarting a thread mid-length is refused, as explained above. This issue stays open as the umbrella until they land.

The Sandvik's CoroPlus OptiThreading was what I was remembering.
